column1: # How the discipline got here. Dates are the entry's sort key; unlinked on purpose.

column3: note
Widely treated as the first fully animated film: drawn line, no photography of objects.
Abstract film in Germany: motion as composition rather than as story.
Visual music. Shape and colour cut to sound, decades before anyone said "motion graphics".
Painting and scratching straight onto film stock. The first camera-less motion design.
Drawn sound, pixilation, and a lifetime of technique invented per film.
Title design becomes authored work: Anatomy of a Murder, Vertigo, North by Northwest.
Fast-cut, hand-lettered titles. Dr. Strangelove set the template for kinetic type.
Mechanical computers driving film cameras. The direct ancestor of procedural motion.
A whole channel of identity design. Motion graphics becomes an industry with clients.
The raster foundation everything else in the pipeline assumed.
Compositing and keyframing on a desktop. The tool that defined the job title.
Accessible 3D for designers, and later MoGraph: procedural motion without scripting.
Title design as graphic authorship again, and the start of the modern title sequence.
Effects language leaks into commercial motion work for a decade.
The field gets a public record, a critical voice, and a job board.
Portfolio distribution moves from showreels on tape to a public URL.
A free, complete 3D pipeline. Two decades later it is a real production option.
Structured motion education outside universities. Bootcamps, cohorts, feedback.
Vector animation ships into apps at any resolution. UI motion becomes a discipline.
Interactive, state-driven animation designed once and run live in product.
Unreal, TouchDesigner and shader work move from experiment to client deliverable.
The tools change weekly. Judgement, taste and direction become the scarce part.
